chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter II
paragraphs: After reaching home Nicholas was at first serious and even glum. He was weighed down by the looming necessity of dealing with the stupid business matters his mother had called him home for. To get the burden off his back as quickly as possible, on the third day after his arrival he went, angry and scowling and refusing to say where he was going, to Mitenka's lodge and demanded a full accounting. But what a "full accounting" might look like, Nicholas knew even less than the frightened and bewildered Mitenka. The interview and review of the books did not last long. The village elder, a peasant representative, and the village clerk, who were waiting in the corridor, heard with a mixture of fear and delight first the young count's voice roaring and snapping and rising louder and louder, and then foul words — terrible words — erupting one after another.
"Thief!... Ungrateful wretch!... I'll hack the dog to pieces! I'm not my father!... Robbing us!..." and so on.

Then with no less fear and delight they watched the young count, red-faced and with bloodshot eyes, drag Mitenka out by the scruff of his neck and apply his boot and knee to his backside with remarkable agility, timing each kick between the words and shouting: "Get out! Never let me see your face here again, you scoundrel!"

Mitenka flew headlong down the six steps and ran off into the shrubbery. (This shrubbery was a well-known refuge for wrongdoers at Otradnoe. Mitenka himself, returning drunk from town, used to hide there, and many of the residents at Otradnoe, hiding from Mitenka, knew of its protective qualities.)
Mitenka's wife and sisters-in-law poked their heads and frightened faces out the door of a room where a bright samovar was boiling and where the steward's high bed stood with its patchwork quilt.
The young count paid them no attention but, breathing hard, strode past with determination and went into the house.

The countess, who heard at once from the maids what had happened at the lodge, was reassured by the thought that their affairs would surely now improve, but at the same time worried about what the excitement might do to her son. She went several times on tiptoe to his door and listened as he lit one pipe after another.
The next day the old count took his son aside and, with an embarrassed smile, said:
"But you know, my dear boy, it's a shame you lost your temper! Mitenka has told me all about it."
"I knew it," thought Nicholas, "I'd never make sense of anything in this crazy world."
"You were angry because he hadn't entered those seven hundred rubles. But they were carried forward — and you didn't look at the other page."
"Papa, he's a crook and a thief! I know he is! And what I did, I did. But if you prefer, I won't say another word to him."

"No, my dear boy" — the count, too, felt embarrassed; he knew he had mismanaged his wife's property and was to blame toward his children, but he didn't know how to fix it — "No, I beg you to take care of the business. I'm old. I..."
"No, Papa. Forgive me if I've upset you. I understand it all even less than you do."

"To hell with all these peasants, and money matters, and carrying things forward from page to page," he thought. "I used to understand what a 'corner' and the stakes at cards meant, but I don't understand carrying forward at all," he told himself, and after that he didn't meddle in business affairs. But once the countess called her son in and told him that she held a promissory note from Anna Mikhaylovna for two thousand rubles, and asked him what he thought they should do with it.

"This," answered Nicholas. "You say it's up to me. Well, I don't like Anna Mikhaylovna and I don't like Boris, but they were our friends and they're poor. So — this!" And he tore up the note, which made the old countess weep tears of joy. After that, young Rostov took no further part in business affairs and threw himself with passionate enthusiasm into what was for him a new pursuit — hunting — for which his father maintained a large establishment.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter III
paragraphs: The weather was already turning wintry and morning frosts hardened the earth, which was saturated from autumn rains. The green of the pastures stood out sharply against the brownish strips of winter rye trampled by cattle, and against the pale yellow stubble of the spring buckwheat. The wooded ravines and copses, still green islands amid the black fields and stubble at the end of August, had turned to golden and crimson islands amid the green winter rye. The hares had already half changed their summer coats, the fox cubs were beginning to scatter, and the young wolves were bigger than dogs. It was the best time of year for the hunt. The hounds of the passionate young sportsman Rostov had not only reached peak winter condition but were so worn out that at a meeting of the huntsmen it was decided to give them three days' rest and then, on the sixteenth of September, to set out on a distant expedition to the oak grove where there was an undisturbed litter of wolf cubs.

All that day the hounds stayed home. It was frosty and the air was sharp, but toward evening the sky clouded over and it began to thaw. On the fifteenth, when young Rostov in his dressing gown looked out the window, he saw the morning was perfect for hunting: the sky seemed to be melting and sinking earthward with no wind at all. The only movement in the air was the slow fall of microscopic droplets of drizzling mist. The bare twigs in the garden were hung with transparent drops that fell on the freshly fallen leaves. The earth in the kitchen garden looked wet and black and glistened like poppy seeds, merging at a short distance into the dull, moist veil of fog. Nicholas went out onto the wet, muddy porch. There was a smell of rotting leaves and of dog. Milka, a black-spotted, broad-haunched bitch with prominent dark eyes, got up on seeing her master, stretched her hind legs, crouched like a hare, and then suddenly leaped up and licked him right on the nose and mustache. Another borzoi, catching sight of his master from the garden path, arched his back and, rushing headlong toward the porch with tail raised, began rubbing himself against his legs.

"O-hoy!" came that inimitable huntsman's call at that moment — the one that blends the deepest bass with the shrillest treble — and around the corner came Daniel, the head huntsman and chief kennelman: a gray, wrinkled old man with hair cut straight across his forehead in the Ukrainian style, a long bent whip in his hand, and that look of independence and scorn for everything that is only found in huntsmen. He doffed his Circassian cap to his master and looked at him contemptuously. This contempt was not offensive to his master. Nicholas knew that this Daniel, who looked down on everyone and considered himself above all of them, was still his serf and his huntsman.

"Daniel!" Nicholas said timidly, conscious at the sight of the weather, the hounds, and the huntsman that he was being swept away by that irresistible passion for the hunt that makes a man forget all his previous resolutions, as a lover forgets everything in the presence of his beloved.

"What are your orders, your excellency?" said the huntsman in his deep bass — deep as a deacon's and hoarse from years of halloing — as two flashing black eyes gazed from beneath his brows at his master, who was saying nothing. "Can you resist it?" those eyes seemed to ask.
"Good day for it, eh? For a hunt and a gallop, eh?" asked Nicholas, scratching Milka behind the ears.
Daniel didn't answer, but winked instead.

"I sent Uvarka out at dawn to listen," his deep voice boomed after a minute's pause. "He says she's moved them into the Otradnoe enclosure. They were howling there." This meant that the she-wolf they both knew about had moved with her cubs into the Otradnoe copse, a small wood about a mile and a half from the house.
"We ought to go, don't you think?" said Nicholas. "Come to me with Uvarka."
"As you wish."
"Then hold off feeding them."
"Yes, sir."

Five minutes later Daniel and Uvarka were standing in Nicholas's large study. Though Daniel was not a big man, seeing him in a room was like seeing a horse or a bear among the furniture and trappings of human life. Daniel felt this himself, and as usual stood just inside the door, trying to speak softly and keep still for fear of breaking something in the master's apartment. He rushed to say everything necessary so he could get out from under that ceiling, back into the open air under the sky.

Having finished his questions and extracted from Daniel the opinion that the hounds were fit — Daniel himself wanted to go — Nicholas ordered the horses saddled. But just as Daniel was about to leave, Natasha came in with quick steps, her hair not done up and her old nurse's big shawl wrapped around her. Petya ran in at the same moment.
"You're going?" asked Natasha. "I knew you would! Sonya said you wouldn't, but I knew that today was the kind of day you couldn't resist."

"Yes, we're going," replied Nicholas reluctantly, for today he planned to hunt seriously and didn't want to bring Natasha and Petya along. "We're going, but only after wolves — it would be dull for you."
"You know it's my greatest pleasure," said Natasha. "It's not fair — you're going off by yourself, having the horses saddled, and you didn't even tell us."
"'No barrier bars a Russian's path' — we're going!" shouted Petya.
"But you can't. Mama said you mustn't," said Nicholas to Natasha.
"Yes, I'll go. I'm definitely going," said Natasha firmly. "Daniel, tell them to saddle up for us, and have Michael come with my dogs," she added to the huntsman.

It seemed irksome and improper to Daniel to be in a room at all, but to deal with a young lady struck him as simply impossible. He lowered his eyes and hurried out as if it were none of his business, careful not to cause any accidental harm to the young lady.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: The old count, who had always maintained an enormous hunting establishment but had now turned it entirely over to his son, was in very good spirits on this fifteenth of September and prepared to join the others.

Within an hour the whole hunting party was assembled at the porch. Nicholas, with a stern and serious air that showed there was no time for trifles, walked past Natasha and Petya, who were trying to tell him something. He inspected every detail of the hunt, sent a pack of hounds and huntsmen ahead to find the quarry, mounted his chestnut Donets, whistled to his own leash of borzois, and set off across the threshing ground toward a field that led to the Otradnoe wood. The old count's horse, a sorrel gelding called Viflynanka, was led by his groom, while the count himself rode in a small trap to a spot reserved for him.

They were taking fifty-four hounds, with six hunt attendants and whippers-in. Besides the family, there were eight borzoi keepers and more than forty borzois, so that — counting the borzois on leash belonging to family members — there were about a hundred and thirty dogs and twenty horsemen.

Each dog knew its master and its name. Each man in the hunt knew his job, his position, and what he had to do. As soon as they passed the fence they all spread out evenly and quietly, without noise or talk, along the road and field leading to the Otradnoe covert.

The horses stepped across the field as over a thick carpet, now and then splashing into puddles as they crossed a road. The misty sky still seemed to be descending evenly and imperceptibly toward the earth; the air was still, warm, and silent. Occasionally the whistle of a huntsman, the snort of a horse, the crack of a whip, or the whine of a straggling hound could be heard.
When they had gone just under a mile, five more riders with dogs appeared out of the mist, approaching the Rostovs. In front rode a fresh-looking, handsome old man with a large gray mustache.
"Good morning, Uncle!" said Nicholas as the old man drew near.

"That's it. Come on!... I was sure of it," began "Uncle." He was a distant relative of the Rostovs', a man of modest means and their neighbor. "I knew you wouldn't be able to resist, and it's a good thing you're going. That's it! Come on!" — this was "Uncle's" favorite expression. "Get to the covert at once — my man Girchik says the Ilagins are at Korniki with their pack. That's it! Come on! They'll snatch the cubs from right under your nose."
"That's where I'm heading. Shall we join up our packs?" asked Nicholas.

The hounds were combined into one pack, and "Uncle" and Nicholas rode on side by side. Natasha, muffled in shawls that couldn't hide her eager face and shining eyes, galloped up to them. She was followed by Petya, who always kept close to her, by Michael the huntsman, and by a groom assigned to look after her. Petya, laughing, kept whipping and tugging at his horse. Natasha sat easily and confidently on her black Arabchik, reining him in with a firm hand.
"Uncle" looked disapprovingly at Petya and Natasha. He didn't like mixing frivolity with the serious business of hunting.
"Good morning, Uncle! We're coming too!" shouted Petya.
"Good morning, good morning! But don't overrun the hounds," said "Uncle" sternly.
"Nicholas, what a wonderful dog Trunila is! He recognized me," said Natasha, referring to her favorite hound.

"First of all, Trunila is not a 'dog' but a harrier," thought Nicholas, and he gave his sister a stern look, trying to make her feel the distance that ought to separate them at this moment. Natasha understood.
"You mustn't think we'll be in anyone's way, Uncle," she said. "We'll go to our spots and won't budge."
"Good idea, little countess," said "Uncle." "Only don't fall off your horse — that's it, come on! — because you've got nothing to hold on to."

The oasis of the Otradnoe covert came into sight a few hundred yards away, and the huntsmen were already nearing it. Rostov, having finally agreed with "Uncle" where to position the hounds and having shown Natasha where to stand — a spot where nothing could possibly break out — rode around above the ravine.
"Well, nephew, you're going after a big wolf," said "Uncle." "Don't let her slip!"

"That's as may be," answered Rostov. "Karay, here!" he shouted, responding to "Uncle's" remark with a call to his borzoi. Karay was a shaggy old dog with a hanging jowl, famous for having tackled a big wolf single-handedly. They all took up their positions.

The old count, knowing his son's passion for the hunt, hurried so as not to be late, and the huntsmen had not yet reached their places when Count Ilya Rostov, cheerful, flushed, and with quivering cheeks, drove up with his black horses over the winter rye to the spot reserved for him, where a wolf might emerge. Having straightened his coat and fastened on his hunting knives and horn, he mounted his good, sleek, well-fed horse Viflynanka — which was turning gray, like himself. His carriage was sent home. Count Ilya Rostov, though not a keen sportsman at heart, knew the rules of the hunt well. He rode to the bushy edge of the road where he was to stand, settled his reins, got comfortable in the saddle, and — feeling he was ready — looked about with a smile.

Beside him was Simon Chekmar, his personal attendant, an old horseman now somewhat stiff in the saddle. Chekmar held in leash three formidable wolfhounds who had, however, grown fat like their master and his horse. Two wise old dogs lay nearby, unleashed. About a hundred paces farther along the edge of the wood stood Mitka, the count's other groom — a daring horseman and enthusiastic rider to hounds. Before the hunt, following an old tradition, the count had drunk a silver cupful of mulled brandy, had a snack, and washed it down with half a bottle of his favorite Bordeaux.

He was a bit flushed from the wine and the drive. His eyes were somewhat moist and glittered more than usual, and as he sat in the saddle wrapped in his fur coat, he looked like a child taken out for a treat.

The thin, hollow-cheeked Chekmar, having gotten everything ready, kept glancing at his master — with whom he had lived on the best of terms for thirty years — and sensing his mood, expected a pleasant chat. A third person rode up cautiously through the wood (clearly he had been taught a lesson) and stopped behind the count. This was a gray-bearded old man in a woman's cloak, with a tall peaked cap on his head. He was the buffoon, who went by a woman's name — Nastasya Ivanovna.
"Well, Nastasya Ivanovna!" the count whispered, winking at him. "If you scare off the quarry, Daniel will give you what for!"
"I know a thing or two myself!" said Nastasya Ivanovna.
"Shh!" whispered the count and turned to Simon. "Have you seen the young countess? Where is she?"
"With young Count Petya, by the Zharov tall grass," answered Simon, smiling. "Though she's a lady, she's very keen on hunting."
"And you're surprised at the way she rides, Simon, eh?" said the count. "She's as good as any man!"
"Of course! It's wonderful. So bold, so easy!"
"And Nicholas? Where is he? By the Lyadov upland, isn't he?"
"Yes, sir. He knows where to stand. He understands the sport so well that Daniel and I are often quite amazed," said Simon, knowing what would please his master.
"Rides well, eh? And how fine he looks on his horse, eh?"

"A perfect picture! The other day he chased a fox out of the tall grass by the Zavarzinsk thicket! He jumped over a terrifying obstacle — what a sight when they burst from the covert! The horse worth a thousand rubles and the rider beyond all price! Yes, you'd have to search far to find another like him."
"Far indeed..." repeated the count, evidently wishing Simon had said more. "Far indeed," he said, turning back the skirt of his coat to reach his snuffbox.

"The other day when he came from church in full uniform, Michael Sidorych..." Simon didn't finish, for on the still air he had clearly caught the sound of the hunt — just two or three hounds giving tongue. He bent his head and listened, raising a warning finger at his master. "They're on the scent of the cubs..." he whispered, "heading straight for the Lyadov uplands."

The count, forgetting to smooth the smile off his face, gazed into the distance down the narrow open space ahead, holding his snuffbox but not taking any. After the cry of the hounds came the deep tones of Daniel's hunting horn calling the wolf; the pack joined the first three hounds and could be heard in full cry, with that special lift in the note that signals they are after a wolf. The whippers-in stopped urging on the hounds and changed to the cry of ulyulyu, and above all the others rose Daniel's voice — now a deep bass, now piercingly shrill. His voice seemed to fill the whole forest and carried far out into the open field.

After listening in silence for a few moments, the count and his attendant could tell that the hounds had split into two packs: the larger pack, giving eager tongue, began to fade in the distance; the other rushed past through the wood near the count, and it was with this second pack that Daniel's voice could be heard calling ulyulyu. The sounds of both packs mingled and broke apart, but both were growing more distant.

Simon sighed and bent down to straighten a leash that a young borzoi had tangled; the count sighed too and, noticing the snuffbox in his hand, opened it and took a pinch. "Back!" cried Simon to a borzoi that was pushing forward out of the wood. The count flinched and dropped the snuffbox. Nastasya Ivanovna dismounted to pick it up. The count and Simon were looking at him.
Then, unexpectedly — as often happens — the sound of the hunt suddenly seemed to rush toward them, as if the hounds in full cry and Daniel calling ulyulyu were right in front of them.
The count turned and saw, on his right, Mitka staring at him with eyes popping out of his head, raising his cap and pointing urgently to the other side.
"Look out!" Mitka shouted, in a voice that showed he had been straining to let that word loose for some time, and releasing the borzois he galloped toward the count.

The count and Simon burst out of the wood and saw to their left a wolf trotting at an easy lope, swaying gently from side to side, heading toward the very spot where they were standing. The angry borzois whined, tore free of their leashes, and dashed past the horses' feet at the wolf.

The wolf paused, turned its heavy head toward the dogs with an awkward motion — like a man with a sore throat — and, still swaying slightly, gave a couple of leaps and, with a swish of its tail, vanished into the edge of the wood. At the same instant, with a cry like a wail, first one hound, then another, then another, came flying helter-skelter from the wood on the opposite side, and the whole pack raced across the field toward the very spot where the wolf had disappeared. The hazel bushes parted behind the hounds, and Daniel's chestnut horse appeared, dark with sweat. On its long back Daniel sat hunched forward, capless, his disheveled gray hair hanging over his flushed, sweating face.
"Ulyulyulyu! Ulyulyu!" he cried. When he spotted the count, his eyes flashed like lightning.
"Damn you!" he shouted, raising his whip threateningly at the count.

"You let the wolf go!... Call yourselves sportsmen!" And as if scorning to waste further words on the frightened and shamefaced count, he lashed the heaving flanks of his sweating chestnut with all the fury the count had provoked and flew off after the hounds. The count, like a punished schoolboy, looked around, trying to win Simon's sympathy with a smile. But Simon was already gone — galloping around through the bushes while the rest of the field closed in from both sides, all trying to head off the wolf. But it vanished into the woods before they could reach it.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter V
paragraphs: Nicholas Rostov meanwhile stayed at his post, waiting for the wolf. From the way the hunt approached and receded, from the cries of the dogs whose voices he knew well, from how the voices of the huntsmen rose and fell, he could tell what was happening at the copse. He knew that young and old wolves were there, that the hounds had split into two packs, that somewhere a wolf was being chased, and that something had gone wrong. He expected the wolf to come his way at any moment. He made a thousand guesses about where and from which side the animal would appear and how he would set upon it. Hope alternated with despair. Several times he found himself praying to God to let the wolf come his way. He prayed with that intense, embarrassed feeling people have when they pray in moments of great excitement over trivial things. "What would it cost You to do this for me?" he said to God. "I know You are great and that it's a sin to ask, but for God's sake let the old wolf come my way, and let Karay spring at its throat — right in front of Uncle, who's watching from over there — and seize it in a death grip!" A thousand times during that half hour Rostov cast eager, restless glances at the edge of the wood with its two scrawny oaks rising above the aspen undergrowth, and the gully with its eroded bank, and Uncle's cap just visible above a bush to his right.

"No, I won't have that luck," thought Rostov. "And yet, what wouldn't it be worth! It's not meant to be! Everywhere — at cards, in war — I'm always unlucky." Memories of Austerlitz and of Dolokhov flashed rapidly through his mind. "Just once in my life to get an old wolf — that's all I ask!" he thought, straining his eyes and ears, looking left and then right, listening for the slightest change in the hounds' cries.

Again he looked to the right and saw something running toward him across the empty field. "No, it can't be!" thought Rostov, drawing a deep breath like someone witnessing the arrival of something long hoped for. The peak of happiness was reached — and so simply, without warning, or noise, or fanfare, that Rostov couldn't believe his eyes and remained in doubt for a full second. The wolf ran forward and jumped heavily over a gully in its path. It was an old animal with a gray back and a big reddish belly. It ran without haste, clearly confident no one had spotted it. Rostov, holding his breath, glanced at the borzois. They stood or lay there, not seeing the wolf, not grasping the situation. Old Karay had turned his head and was angrily snapping at fleas, baring his yellow teeth and nipping at his hind legs.

"Ulyulyulyu!" Rostov whispered, pursing his lips. The borzois jumped up, jerking their leash-rings and pricking their ears. Karay finished scratching, cocked his ears, and stood up with quivering tail, tufts of matted hair hanging from his thigh.

"Should I release them or not?" Nicholas asked himself as the wolf approached from the copse. Suddenly the wolf's whole expression changed: it shuddered, seeing what it had probably never seen before — human eyes fixed upon it — and, turning its head slightly toward Rostov, it paused.
"Forward or back? No matter — forward..." the wolf seemed to decide, and it moved on without another backward glance, in a quiet, long, easy but resolute lope.

"Ulyulyu!" cried Nicholas in a voice not his own, and of its own accord his good horse plunged headlong downhill, leaping over gullies to cut off the wolf, and the borzois raced past even faster. Nicholas didn't hear his own shout, didn't feel himself galloping, didn't see the borzois or the ground beneath him — he saw only the wolf, which quickened its pace and bounded in the same direction along the hollow. The first to come into view was Milka, with her black markings and powerful hindquarters, gaining on the wolf. Closer and closer... now she was alongside. But the wolf turned its head to face her, and instead of putting on speed as she usually did, Milka suddenly raised her tail and braced her front legs.
"Ulyulyulyulyu!" shouted Nicholas.

The reddish Lyubim rushed forward from behind Milka, sprang boldly at the wolf, and seized it by the haunches — but instantly jumped away in terror. The wolf crouched, snapped its jaws, and rose again, bounding forward. All the borzois followed at a distance of a couple of feet but couldn't close the gap.
"She'll get away! No, it's impossible!" thought Nicholas, still shouting in a hoarse voice.

"Karay, ulyulyu!" he called, looking around for the old borzoi who was now his only hope. Karay, with all the strength his age still allowed, stretched himself to the utmost and, watching the wolf, galloped heavily at an angle to cut it off. But the wolf's speed and the borzoi's slower pace made it clear that Karay had misjudged the angle. Nicholas could already see the woods not far ahead — the wolf would certainly escape if it reached them. But coming toward him from that direction he saw hounds and a huntsman galloping almost straight at the wolf. There was still hope. A long, yellowish young borzoi that Nicholas didn't recognize — from another leash — rushed at the wolf from the front and nearly knocked it over. But the wolf recovered faster than anyone could have expected and, snapping its jaws, flew at the yellowish borzoi, which fell with a piercing yelp, its head hitting the ground, blood pouring from a gash in its side.
"Karay! Old boy!..." wailed Nicholas.

Thanks to the delay caused by the young borzoi's charge, old Karay, with his matted hair hanging from his thigh, had closed to within five paces. As if sensing its danger, the wolf glanced at Karay, tucked its tail even tighter between its legs, and ran faster. But at that moment Nicholas saw something happen to Karay — the borzoi was suddenly on top of the wolf, and together they tumbled into a gully just ahead.

That instant — when Nicholas saw the wolf struggling in the gully with the dogs while from beneath them he could make out its gray fur and outstretched hind leg and its frightened, choking head with ears laid back, Karay pinning it by the throat — was the happiest moment of his life. With his hand on the saddlebow, he was ready to dismount and stab the wolf when it suddenly thrust its head up from the mass of dogs and got its front paws onto the edge of the gully. It clicked its teeth — Karay no longer had it by the throat — and with a movement of its hind legs leaped out of the gully. Having shaken off the dogs, it tucked its tail in again and loped forward. Karay, his fur bristling and probably bruised or hurt, climbed with difficulty out of the gully.
"Oh my God! Why?" Nicholas cried in despair.
"Uncle's" huntsman was galloping from the other side to block the wolf's path, and his borzois once more stopped its advance. It was hemmed in again.

Nicholas, his attendant, "Uncle," and his huntsman were all riding around the wolf, shouting "ulyulyu!" and preparing to dismount each time the wolf crouched back, then surging forward again each time it shook itself free and headed for the wood where it would be safe.

Already at the beginning of the chase, Daniel — hearing the ulyulyuing — had burst out of the wood. He had seen Karay seize the wolf and checked his horse, thinking the business was over. But when he saw that the horsemen weren't dismounting and the wolf had shaken itself free and was heading for safety, Daniel set his chestnut galloping — not toward the wolf, but straight for the wood, to cut it off, just as Karay had tried to do. Thanks to this he galloped up to the wolf just as it was being stopped a second time by "Uncle's" borzois.
Daniel rode up in silence, holding a naked dagger in his left hand and lashing the laboring sides of his chestnut horse with his whip as if it were a flail.

Nicholas neither saw nor heard Daniel until the chestnut, breathing heavily, panted past him, and he heard the thud of a body falling and saw Daniel lying on the wolf's back among the dogs, trying to seize it by the ears. It was clear to the dogs, the hunters, and to the wolf itself that all was now over. The terrified wolf pressed back its ears and tried to rise, but the borzois clung to it. Daniel got up slightly, took a step, and with his whole weight — as if lying down to rest — threw himself on the wolf, seizing it by the ears. Nicholas was about to stab it, but Daniel whispered: "Don't! We'll muzzle it!" Shifting his position, he planted his foot on the wolf's neck. A stick was thrust between its jaws and it was tied up with a leash, like a bridle; its legs were bound together, and Daniel rolled it over once or twice.

With happy, exhausted faces they loaded the live old wolf onto a rearing, snorting horse and, accompanied by dogs yelping at it, carried it to the meeting place. The hounds had killed two of the cubs and the borzois three. The huntsmen gathered with their trophies and their stories, and everyone came to look at the wolf, which, with its broad-browed head hanging down and the bitten stick clamped between its jaws, stared with large, glassy eyes at the crowd of dogs and men surrounding it. When someone touched it, it jerked its bound legs and looked at them all with a wild yet simple gaze. Old Count Rostov rode up too and touched the wolf.
"Oh, what a brute!" he said. "A real brute, eh?" he asked Daniel, who was standing nearby.
"Yes, your excellency," answered Daniel, quickly doffing his cap.
The count remembered the wolf he had let slip and his encounter with Daniel.
"Ah, but you are a crusty fellow, friend!" said the count.
For his only reply, Daniel gave him a shy, childlike, meek, and endearing smile.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: The old count went home, and Natasha and Petya promised to return very soon, but since it was still early the hunt continued. At midday they put the hounds into a ravine thickly overgrown with young trees. Nicholas, standing in a fallow field, could see all his whips.

Facing him lay a field of winter rye; there his own huntsman stood alone in a hollow behind a hazel bush. The hounds had barely been released before Nicholas heard a familiar hound, Voltorn, giving tongue at intervals; others joined in, now pausing and now sounding again. A moment later a cry came from the wooded ravine that a fox had been found, and the whole pack, joining together, raced along the ravine toward the rye field and away from Nicholas.
He could see the whips in their red caps galloping along the edge of the ravine; he even caught sight of the hounds, and was expecting a fox to appear any moment on the rye field opposite.

The huntsman in the hollow moved and released his borzois, and Nicholas saw a strange, short-legged red fox with a fine brush running hard across the field. The borzois bore down on it... They drew close to the fox, which started dodging in tighter and tighter curves, trailing its brush — when suddenly a strange white borzoi dashed in, followed by a black one, and everything was confusion. The borzois formed a star-shaped cluster, barely swaying their bodies and with tails pointing away from the center. Two huntsmen galloped up to the dogs — one in a red cap, the other, a stranger, in a green coat.
"What's going on?" thought Nicholas. "Where did that huntsman come from? He's not one of Uncle's men."

The huntsmen secured the fox but stayed there for a long time without tying it to the saddle. Their horses, bridled and with high saddles, stood nearby, and the dogs lay on the ground. The huntsmen were waving their arms and doing something with the fox. Then from that spot came the blast of a horn — the signal agreed upon in case of a fight.
"That's Ilagin's huntsman having a row with our Ivan," said Nicholas's groom.
Nicholas sent the man to call Natasha and Petya and rode at a walk toward where the whips were gathering the hounds. Several riders from the field galloped toward the spot of the fight.

Nicholas dismounted, and with Natasha and Petya, who had ridden up, stood near the hounds, waiting to see how the matter would end. Out of the bushes rode the huntsman who had been fighting, heading for his young master with the fox tied to his crupper. While still some distance away he took off his cap and tried to speak respectfully, but his face was pale and he was breathing hard, and his expression was furious. One eye was black, though he probably didn't even realize it.
"What happened?" asked Nicholas.

"A likely story — killing a fox our dogs had hunted! And it was my gray bitch that caught it! Go to court if you like!... He grabs at the fox! I gave him one with the fox across the face. Here it is, on my saddle! Want a taste of this?" said the huntsman, pointing to his dagger, probably imagining he was still talking to his enemy.
Nicholas, without stopping to hear more, asked his sister and Petya to wait for him and rode toward the place where the rival — Ilagin's — hunting party was.
The victorious huntsman rode off to join the field and there, surrounded by curious well-wishers, recounted his exploits.

The facts were that Ilagin — with whom the Rostovs had a quarrel and were in litigation — hunted over lands that belonged by custom to the Rostovs, and had now, as if deliberately, sent his men to the very woods the Rostovs were hunting and let his huntsman snatch a fox their dogs had chased.

Nicholas, though he had never met Ilagin, with his usual lack of moderation in passing judgment, hated him with all his heart based on reports of his high-handedness and violence, and regarded him as his worst enemy. He rode toward him in furious agitation, gripping his whip, fully prepared to take the most extreme and desperate action to punish his foe.
He had barely passed the corner of the wood when a stout gentleman in a beaver cap came riding toward him on a handsome raven-black horse, accompanied by two hunt servants.

Instead of the enemy he expected, Nicholas found in Ilagin a dignified and courteous gentleman who was especially eager to make the young count's acquaintance. Riding up, Ilagin raised his beaver cap and said he deeply regretted what had happened and would punish the man who had allowed himself to seize a fox hunted by someone else's borzois. He expressed his hope of becoming better acquainted with the count and invited him to hunt his own covert.

Natasha, who had been afraid her brother would do something terrible, had followed him nervously. Seeing the two enemies exchanging friendly greetings, she rode up to them. Ilagin raised his beaver cap even higher to Natasha and said, with a pleasant smile, that the young countess reminded him of Diana, both in her passion for the hunt and in her beauty, of which he had heard much.

To atone for his huntsman's offense, Ilagin urged the Rostovs to come to a stretch of upland about a mile away that he usually kept for himself and which, he said, was teeming with hares. Nicholas agreed, and the hunt, now doubled in size, moved on.

The way to Ilagin's ground led across open fields. The hunt servants fell into line. The masters rode together. "Uncle," Rostov, and Ilagin kept stealing glances at one another's dogs, trying not to be noticed by their companions, and anxiously searching for rivals to their own borzois.

Rostov was particularly struck by the beauty of a small, purebred, red-spotted bitch on Ilagin's leash — slender, but with muscles like steel, a delicate muzzle, and prominent black eyes. He had heard of the speed of Ilagin's borzois, and in that beautiful bitch he saw a rival to his own Milka.
In the middle of a serious conversation about the year's harvest, Nicholas pointed to the red-spotted bitch.
"A fine little bitch, that!" he said casually. "Is she fast?"

"That one? Yes, she's a good dog — catches what she's after," answered Ilagin offhandedly, speaking of the bitch Erza, for which he had paid a neighbor three families of house serfs the year before. "So in your area too the harvest is nothing to boast about, Count?" he went on, continuing their earlier conversation. And thinking it polite to return the young count's compliment, Ilagin looked over his borzois and picked out Milka, which caught his eye with her powerful build. "That black-spotted one of yours is nice — well shaped!" he said.

"Yes, she's fast enough," replied Nicholas, and thought: "If only a full-grown hare would cross the field right now, I'd show you what kind of borzoi she is." Turning to his groom, he said he'd give a ruble to anyone who flushed a hare.

"I don't understand," continued Ilagin, "how some sportsmen can get so jealous about game and dogs. Personally, I can tell you, Count, I enjoy riding in company like this — what could be better?" He again raised his cap to Natasha. "But as for counting skins and keeping score, I don't care about any of that."
"Of course not!"
"Or getting upset because someone else's borzoi, not mine, catches something. All I care about is enjoying the chase — isn't that right, Count? Because I think that..."

"A-tu!" came the long-drawn cry of one of the borzoi whippers-in, who had stopped on a rise in the stubble. He stood on a hillock, holding his whip aloft, and again drew out his cry: "A-tu!" This call and the raised whip meant he had spotted a sitting hare.

"Ah, I think he's found one," said Ilagin casually. "Yes, let's ride up... Shall we both course it?" replied Nicholas, seeing in Erza and in "Uncle's" red Rugay two rivals he had never before had the chance to pit against his own borzois. "What if they outrun my Milka right away!" he thought as he rode with "Uncle" and Ilagin toward the hare.
"A full-grown one?" asked Ilagin as he approached the whip who had sighted the hare — and not without excitement he glanced around and whistled to Erza.
"And you, Michael Nikanorych?" he said, addressing "Uncle."
"Uncle" was riding with a grim expression.
"How can I compete? Why, you've paid a fortune for each of your borzois! That's it — come on! Yours are worth thousands. You two match your dogs against each other — I'll just watch!"

"Rugay, hey, hey!" he shouted. "Rugayushka!" he added, involuntarily using the diminutive to express his affection and the hopes he placed on this red borzoi. Natasha could see and feel the excitement the two older men and her brother were trying to hide, and was caught up in it herself.

The huntsman stood halfway up the hillock with his whip raised; the gentlemen rode up at a walk. The hounds far off on the horizon turned away from the hare, and the whips, but not the gentlemen, also moved aside. Everyone was moving slowly and deliberately.
"Which way is it pointing?" asked Nicholas, riding a hundred paces toward the whip.

But before the whip could answer, the hare — sensing the frost that was coming the next morning — could no longer sit still and leaped up. The pack on leash surged downhill in full cry after the hare, and from all directions the unleashed borzois charged after the hounds and the hare. All the hunters who had been moving slowly now shouted "Stop!" calling back the hounds, while the borzoi whippers-in galloped across the field with a cry of "A-tu!" setting the borzois loose. The composed Ilagin, Nicholas, Natasha, and "Uncle" flew forward, caring nothing for where or how they went, seeing only the borzois and the hare, and terrified of losing sight of the chase for even an instant. The hare they had started was a strong and swift one. When it jumped up it didn't bolt immediately but pricked its ears, listening to the shouts and pounding hooves from every side. It took a dozen bounds, not very fast, letting the borzois gain — and then, having chosen its direction and grasped the danger, laid back its ears and shot off at top speed. It had been lying in the stubble, but ahead of it was the autumn planting where the ground was soft. The two borzois of the huntsman who had spotted it, being closest, were first to see and pursue it, but they hadn't gone far before Ilagin's red-spotted Erza passed them, closed to within a length, and flew at the hare with terrifying speed, aiming at its tail — and, thinking she had seized it, tumbled head over heels like a ball. The hare arched its back and bounded off even faster. From behind, the broad-haunched, black-spotted Milka came rapidly gaining.

"Milashka, darling!" rose Nicholas's triumphant shout. It looked as if Milka would pounce on the hare any second, but she overtook it and shot past. The hare had squatted. Again the beautiful Erza caught up, but when close to the hare's tail she hesitated — as if measuring the distance, so as not to make the same mistake twice — and tried to seize its hind leg.

"Erza, darling!" Ilagin wailed in a voice unlike his own. Erza didn't listen. At the very instant she would have caught her prey, the hare swerved and darted along the boundary strip between the winter rye and the stubble. Again Erza and Milka ran neck and neck, like a pair of carriage horses, and started to overtake the hare. But it was easier for the hare to run on the strip, and the borzois didn't gain as quickly.

"Rugay, Rugayushka! That's it — come on!" came a third voice just then, and "Uncle's" red borzoi, straining and arching its back, caught up with the two leaders, pushed past them both, put on a burst of savage speed close to the hare, knocked it off the strip onto the rye field, surged forward even more ferociously — sinking to its knees in the muddy ground — and all one could see was how, covered in mud, it rolled over with the hare. A ring of borzois gathered around. A moment later everyone had ridden up. Only the elated "Uncle" dismounted and cut off a paw, shaking the hare so the blood dripped off, glancing around with restless eyes while his arms and legs twitched. He spoke without knowing whom he was addressing or what he was saying. "That's it — come on! There's a dog for you!... Beat them all — the thousand-ruble ones and the one-ruble ones alike. That's it — come on!" he said, panting, looking around furiously as if they were all his enemies who had insulted him, and only now had he at last vindicated himself. "There go your thousand-ruble borzois... That's it — come on!"
"Rugay, here's a paw for you!" he said, tossing down the hare's muddy foot. "You earned it — that's it — come on!"
"She'd tired herself out — she'd run it down three times on her own," said Nicholas, also not listening to anyone and not caring whether he was heard.
"But what's the trick in running across it like that?" said Ilagin's groom.

"Once she'd missed it and turned it away, any mutt could have caught it," Ilagin was saying at the same time, breathless from the gallop and the excitement. At that same moment Natasha, without stopping to breathe, let out a shriek — so joyous, so ecstatic, and so piercing that it set everyone's ears ringing. With that shriek she expressed what all the others were expressing by talking at once, and it was so wild that she herself would normally have been mortified by it, and everyone else would have been astonished at any other time. "Uncle" himself tucked the hare neatly and smartly across his horse's back — as if rebuking everyone with the gesture — and, with an air of not wanting to speak to anyone, mounted his bay and rode away. All the others followed, deflated and shamefaced, and only much later were they able to resume their former pretense of indifference. For a long time they kept looking at the red Rugay, who trotted along behind "Uncle's" horse with his arched, mud-spattered back and the ring of his leash clanking — walking with the serene air of a conqueror.
"Well, I'm like any other dog when it's not a matter of coursing. But when it is — watch out!" his appearance seemed to say to Nicholas.
When, much later, "Uncle" rode up to Nicholas and began to talk, he felt flattered that after what had happened "Uncle" condescended to speak to him.
